Two groups from a grouping procedure, X and Y, are shown below with their true sizes and how many records of each are shown. One pair known to describe the same real-world entity landed on opposite sides. Name a change to the grouping — as a condition on record fields — that would reunite pairs like this one without pulling in many records that do not belong.

Group X holds 15 records, of which 5 are shown. Group Y holds 24 records, of which 8 are shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 15 records, of which 5 are shown. Group Y holds 24 records, of which 8 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 73 records, of which 26 are shown. Group Y holds 128 records, of which 45 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 146 records, of which 51 are shown. Group Y holds 37 records, of which 13 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 85 records, of which 30 are shown. Group Y holds 71 records, of which 25 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 88 records, of which 31 are shown. Group Y holds 155 records, of which 54 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 76 records, of which 27 are shown. Group Y holds 129 records, of which 45 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 75 records, of which 26 are shown. Group Y holds 39 records, of which 14 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 77 records, of which 27 are shown. Group Y holds 117 records, of which 41 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 72 records, of which 25 are shown. Group Y holds 46 records, of which 16 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 85 records, of which 30 are shown. Group Y holds 129 records, of which 45 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 78 records, of which 27 are shown. Group Y holds 143 records, of which 50 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 63 records, of which 22 are shown. Group Y holds 134 records, of which 47 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 79 records, of which 28 are shown. Group Y holds 148 records, of which 52 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 127 records, of which 44 are shown. Group Y holds 132 records, of which 46 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 30 records, of which 10 are shown. Group Y holds 102 records, of which 36 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],

Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 148 records, of which 52 are shown. Group Y holds 133 records, of which 47 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 127 records, of which 44 are shown. Group Y holds 87 records, of which 30 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 166 records, of which 58 are shown. Group Y holds 134 records, of which 47 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

Method:

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 147 records, of which 51 are shown. Group Y holds 139 records, of which 49 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.

Reply with one JSON object. One rule:
{"operation": "move_to_x" | "move_to_y" | "new_block" | "none",
 "predicate": [{"field": "<field name>", "operator": "equals" | "contains" | "not_contains" | "regex" | "is_null" | "is_not_null" | "gte" | "lte" | "between", "value": "<text>"}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Or up to five rules at once, applied in order, each acting on the grouping the earlier rules left:
{"actions": [{"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}, {"operation": "...", "predicate": [...]}],
 "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Operator notes: "contains" is a case-insensitive text match on the field; "regex" is a full regular expression on the field; "gte" and "lte" compare the first number found in the field to "value"; "between" takes "value": [low, high] and is true when the number lies in the range, endpoints included. Conditions within one rule are combined with AND. Field names must be ones that actually appear in the records shown.

1. Set the two seed records beside each other and find the longest stretch of text they carry word-for-word — a full title, a product name, a paper name, a model code. Copy that stretch verbatim from one of the two, keeping its case and punctuation. The "contains" operator matches without regard to case, so you do not need to alter what you copy.

2. Steer clear of short generic tokens as a sole condition: a bare manufacturer name, a bare venue name, a lone author surname, a single common word, a year. Each sweeps in many unrelated records and rarely pays back what it costs.

3. Read the phrase you copied against the other group's sample. If several records there carry the same phrase but are clearly different entities (a shared series title, a co-authored paper's title reused on other papers, a product line shared across items), add a second field condition inside the same rule. The two conditions are joined by AND. Only add a second condition if the field it names is present in both seed records — a condition on a field absent from the seed pair usually matches zero.

4. Prefer "contains" over "equals". "equals" needs the whole field value identical, including trailing punctuation and case, and often matches nothing when the two representations differ by a period or a spacing change.

5. Choose the direction by the group sizes in Group X holds 58 records, of which 20 are shown. Group Y holds 135 records, of which 47 are shown.. Moving a few records out of a much larger group into a smaller one both reunites the pair and lowers the total number of within-group comparisons. If the entity clearly belongs with the smaller group, pick the move that takes it there. The labels X and Y are arbitrary — internal id order, no meaning.

6. "new_block" pulls records satisfying the condition, from either group, into a group of their own. Reach for it when the matching subset looks like one coherent entity but neither X nor Y as they stand is a clean home for it.

7. If nothing in the two seed records is specific enough to write a condition that would not also match unrelated records, answer "none". A no-op costs zero; a broad guess usually costs more than it earns.

Scoring, in one line: for every separated same-entity pair your condition reunites anywhere in the collection you gain credit; you pay five times the relative growth in within-group comparisons. A rule matching one to a few records is almost always safe. A rule matching twenty or more records has to reunite same-entity records in the great majority of cases, or it loses more than it earns.
